sm: Ben opens with clips of the Treasury Secretary saying his department had pushed for months to put the chip company Megaspeed on a restricted list, while the Commerce Department held the pen. He frames this as a growing scandal that is hurting both the AI industry and the Trump administration. Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang has been ousted, and Reuters reports he had an affair with a third, unidentified person. Ben says the affair is not the real reason he is out.

Ben lays out possible explanations, including the suspicion that Huang's relationship with a woman tied to a Chinese-linked firm compromised national security. He reviews export controls on advanced chips and the loophole where a company sells to a Malaysian or Singaporean firm that rents capacity to Chinese customers. Huang has long defended selling chips to China, and Ben argues his self-interest matches his politics. He cites reporting that Singapore's share of Nvidia revenue jumped from 8 percent to 22 percent, and asks whether Megaspeed was a Chinese front company.

Ben plays Attorney General Todd Blanche saying no conclusions have been reached about whether Huang's partner was a spy, and notes it is not clear she was one. CNN reports officials disagree about the evidence, and that the FBI told lawmakers last year it was suspicious of her. Ben argues that even without proof of spying, allowing sophisticated chips to flow to China was an independent policy decision. He says the question is how the administration reached it.

Reporting describes Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnik resisting restrictions, with Trump reportedly directing him three times to pursue them. Elon Musk was consulted and supported Secretary of State Rubio's position before Trump agreed to move forward. Treasury Secretary Bessent is described as deeply unhappy with Lutnik, and commentators say Lutnik should be pushed out. Ben says an AI scandal is turning into a governmental one, and that cozy corporatist policy breeds improper relationships. He adds that the episode could build bipartisan momentum for stricter chip controls and speaks of Chinese technology theft and influence at American universities.

Representative Moolenaar, chair of the House Select Committee on China, calls for export controls and says Huang's firing was avoidable. Ben says Nvidia will take a heavy hit and that Trump is looking for a way to respond. Some suggest Huang stepped down as a heat shield. Ben discusses reporting on Huang's tensions with his finance chief and on aggressive deals that propped up customers, including a giant data center and investment in OpenAI. Nvidia shares fell about 5 percent, and some employees want Huang back.

Ben says Democrats should work with Republicans on not shipping advanced chips to China. He then turns to a New York Times interview in which Ezra Klein discusses a book about Chairman Mao, and criticizes it as too sympathetic. He argues that streamer Hasan Piker, who has a Chinese flag behind him, shows why Democrats should break from their far-left allies.

Ben plays a November 2025 clip of Hasan Piker comparing American and Chinese systems and arguing that consumerism is its own form of control. He then plays Piker saying on Ezra Klein's show that there is no difference between a KKK member and a certain kind of Zionist. Ben says that if the Democratic Party moves in that direction it reopens the door for Republicans. He notes that corruption was a top issue for voters in recent elections, ahead of cost of living, and says the administration should stay clear of it.

Ben covers a Stephen Miller memo reported by Politico and Republican failures to message against socialist candidates. He discusses Senator Chris Van Hollen being floated for Senate leadership and Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed pushing the party left. He recounts Van Hollen's trip to check on a constituent, Kilmar Abrego Garcia. He ends by mocking a controversy over a politician being sworn in on a Quran tied to Thomas Jefferson's copy.

Ben says his new movie Confession was released this week and is based on a 1938 Soviet interrogation. He interviews Ignat Solzhenitsyn, who oversees the legacy of his father, Alexander Solzhenitsyn. They discuss how the elder Solzhenitsyn became an international hero and why socialism fails: it assumes no innate worth in individuals and tries to sever human bonds except economic ones. Ignat says socialism ignores that people are created by God.

They talk about how Ignat handles his father's unpublished works, many untranslated, including the unfinished novel Love the Revolution, which he released while saying plainly that it is unfinished. Ben asks whether young people today have the language to condemn socialism when many think only of welfare programs. Ignat says the novel's themes remain relevant, and that young people drawn to the idea need to learn what it unleashed. He suggests starting points and names the book as Love the Revolution.

Ben jokes that after serious topics he will cover the Call Her Daddy controversy, with the Daily Wire's Lyndon Blake. They discuss the podcast's raunchy content, Sophia Franklin's earlier clash with Barstool and Dave Portnoy, and Franklin's memoir Daddy Issues. Franklin says she did not want to work at Barstool and that the dispute fell apart over valuation.

Lyndon recounts the memoir's claims: that Alex Cooper's content was largely written by a high school friend, who took jokes from elsewhere online, and that Franklin struggled with substance abuse. She describes a sexual assault allegation and a falling out. Lyndon and Ben say the show taught young women damaging ideas about relationships while the real beneficiaries were bad men, and that the story matters because so many people listened.
sg: Ignat Solzhenitsyn on Communism and Legacy
